QA1401.question: Paper 1 shows that the semi-linear Trousers T in R^3 admits no minimum CAD because two distinct minimal CADs cannot be merged into a common coarser one. Using the topological criterion developed in Paper 2 for when three consecutive sector/section cells can be glued into a single closure-coherent piece, explain why the Trousers construction necessarily fails this criterion, and state what property of T's geometry causes the failure.
QA1401.answer: In Paper 1, the Trousers T is defined so that the third coordinate equals 0 on the region (x≤0 ∨ y≤0) and equals -x/2 on the region (x>0 ∧ y>0); any candidate minimal CAD that tries to merge the sectors and section straddling this jump into one piece requires gluing three cylinder cells via a single continuous semi-algebraic function on the merged base, and the two minimal CADs C and C' arise precisely because no such continuous gluing exists across the corner at the origin, forcing at least two incompatible ways to place the section (giving infinitely many minimal CADs, by Proposition 4.6). Paper 2's Lemma 2.3 gives the general reason such a merge can fail: for a sector-section-sector triple A = S⊙(f1,f2), B = S⊙{f2}, C = S⊙(f2,f3), the equality B = closure(A) ∩ closure(C) needed to treat A∪B∪C as closure-coherent holds only when the full sector A∪B∪C is locally boundary connected; Remark 3.6 explicitly notes that its counterexample function is reminiscent of the Trousers of [12] (Paper 1) and exhibits a point in closure(A)∩closure(C) not lying in B. Thus the Trousers' failure to admit a minimum CAD is a concrete instance of the general local-boundary-connectedness obstruction identified in Paper 2: the jump in T's defining piecewise value at x=0,y=0 makes the corresponding sector not locally boundary connected, so the closure-based gluing needed for a unique minimal (hence minimum) CAD cannot occur.

QA1402.question: Paper 1's proof that every 2-dimensional CAD family has a minimum relies on gluing three neighboring section/sector-defining functions into one continuous function across a shared boundary point. Paper 2's Lemma 2.3 shows that merging a sector-section-sector triple A∪B∪C only has closure equal to the union of the individual closures when the merged sector is locally boundary connected. Is Paper 1's R^2 merging technique actually invoking this local-boundary-connectedness condition, or is it a distinct mechanism, and does that distinction affect whether it could be reused to justify the R^4 counterexamples of Paper 2?
QA1402.answer: They are distinct mechanisms operating at different structural levels. Paper 1's Theorem 4.1 merges C_{2i-1}, C_{2i}, C_{2i+1} in R^2 by showing the restrictions of the defining semi-algebraic functions agree at the meeting points ξ_2i (via Corollary 3.5), so the glued function is continuous simply because it locally coincides with a continuous function near every point of its domain — a pointwise functional-continuity argument requiring no separate topological hypothesis on closures. Paper 2's Lemma 2.3, by contrast, is a statement purely about point-set closures of sectors/sections and only guarantees B = A̅∩C̅ (rather than the always-true inclusion B ⊆ A̅∩C̅) when the combined sector A∪B∪C is locally boundary connected; Remark 3.6 shows this can fail without that hypothesis. Because Paper 1's low-dimensional gluing never needs to verify local boundary connectedness (it works directly from continuity of the ξ-functions), it cannot be transplanted to certify closure-based merging in the R^4 exotic sectors of Paper 2, where the relevant sets (e.g. the slit disk-based sectors) are explicitly not locally boundary connected and hence Lemma 2.3's stronger closure identity is unavailable.

QA1403.question: Paper 1's Trousers T and Paper 2's cornet-cell/slit-disk sector both fail a boundary-connectivity property at a single distinguished point (the origin), and this failure is exactly what drives each paper's counterexample. What invariant does the failure break in each case, and how does the shared 'bad point' mechanism differ in its consequence for the two papers' respective conjectures?
QA1403.answer: In Paper 1, the Trousers T is built so that gluing the sector/section functions across the origin of the first-level cylinder produces a discontinuous function (Example 5.11 shows the candidate merged section D_112 is not continuous, since the tree-reduction Ψ_12/Ψ_32 cannot lift to an actual CAD reduction); the bad point is where distinct minimal CADs disagree on how to slice near x=0, and this is what blocks uniqueness, hence blocks existence of a minimum CAD. In Paper 2, the slit disk D_s (equiregular to the cornet cell) is explicitly not locally boundary connected at the origin, and this failure is what lets a sector D_s⊙(-ũ,ũ) bounded above and below by regular sections (each equiregular to a half-disk) itself fail to be regular: removing the origin from the sector leaves a set that deformation-retracts onto a punctured disk, which is not simply connected, unlike a punctured ball, disproving Conjecture 7.2.2. So in both papers a single boundary point where continuity/connectivity fails is the source of a counterexample, but in Paper 1 it breaks global uniqueness of merging (minimum CAD existence), while in Paper 2 it breaks a purely local regularity property of one cell (regular bounds not implying regular sector).

QA1404.question: Paper 1 shows every finite family of semi-algebraic sets in R or R^2 has a unique minimum adapted CAD, but this fails already in R^3 (the Trousers example). Paper 2 recalls that closure-finiteness and well-borderedness of CADs coincide up through dimension 3, and only diverge starting in dimension 4. Since both are 'good behavior' thresholds for CADs, why does dimension 3 still guarantee CF/WB coincidence while already failing to guarantee a minimum adapted CAD?
QA1404.answer:
The two thresholds govern unrelated invariants. Minimum-CAD existence (Paper 1) depends on whether all minimal CADs adapted to a family coincide, which Theorem 4.1 proves automatically in dimension 1 and 2 by gluing boundary-defining functions across merge points, but the Trousers T in R^3 already admits two distinct minimal CADs (Theorem 4.4), so uniqueness of minimal refinements breaks at n=3. CF/WB coincidence (Paper 2) instead concerns whether a single cell's closure decomposes into cells one dimension lower; Locatelli's results (cited in Paper 2) show this still holds for every CAD up to n=3, and only in R^4 can one build a sliced cylinder over a 3-cell with a function f satisfying the boundary-behaviour conditions (i)-(ii) of Theorem 2.2, producing a closure-finite but non-well-bordered CAD. The well-borderedness property is stronger
than the closure finiteness property.So dimension 3 is already high enough to break minimal-CAD uniqueness (a global comparison of decompositions) while still being too low to decouple the purely local closure-structure invariants CF and WB, which require the extra freedom of a fourth coordinate.
QA1404.relation: The dimensional threshold for Paper 1's minimum-CAD phenomenon and Paper 2's CF/WB coincidence phenomenon can only be compared and distinguished by combining both papers' explicit dimension-indexed results.
QA1404.derived_conclusion: Dimension-3 CADs already fail to guarantee a minimum adapted CAD (a global uniqueness property) even though they still guarantee coincidence of closure-finiteness and well-borderedness (a local closure-structure property), showing these are independent notions of 'good CAD behavior.'

The fixed-geometry approach with normal resistance RN ~ 3 kΩ determined by oxide thickness enables reproducible energy scales. In contrast, STM geometry produces variable capacitance C from ~10 fF at Rn = 10 kΩ to ~1 fF at lower Rn, extracted from βc = (Iqp/Ir)² and C = 4βcℏ/(2eIqpR²eπ). The tip-sample separation controls both Rn and C simultaneously: decreasing separation reduces Rn from 10 MΩ to 1 kΩ while increasing C due to reduced gap. This allows tuning from EC >> EJ (phase diffusion regime at high Rn) through EC ~ EJ (quantum regime) to EC << EJ (point contact at Rn < 3 kΩ). The STM's in-situ tunability spans decades of resistance but lacks the geometric control needed for fixed-capacitance qubit applications, whereas Manhattan-style lithography sacrifices tunability for reproducible quantum-regime operation at predetermined energy scales.

QA1415.question: Both the submicron SIsFS ferromagnetic Josephson junctions and the Nb STM Josephson junctions show a switching current Isw far below the theoretical critical current Ic, yet they are classified into different damping regimes using the Stewart-McCumber parameter βc. In the Nb STM junctions, βc = (Iqp/Ir)^2 is much greater than 1 for all measured Rn, formally placing the junctions in the underdamped limit, yet the measured switching current (e.g. 620 pA at Rn=57 kΩ) is still two orders of magnitude below the MAR-theory-predicted Ic (26 nA), attributed to macroscopic quantum tunneling of the phase (Tesc ≈ ħωp/7.2kB ≈1 K) rather than to phase diffusion mediated by a low quality factor. Thus a large βc (underdamped) does not preclude strong Isw suppression: both papers show that even in nominally low-dissipation, high-βc junctions, quantum fluctuation processes (QPD in one case, MQT in the other) can drive Isw well below Ic, meaning the βc classification alone is insufficient to predict the degree of switching-current suppression.

QA1416.question: Submicron ferromagnetic junctions with EC ~ 40 µeV show switching currents Isw ~ 30% of the fluctuation-free critical current Ic, while STM junctions with similar Rn exhibit Is ranging from 1-10% of MAR-predicted Ic. This 70% reduction reflects quantum phase diffusion reducing the effective barrier. In contrast, STM junctions in the range 10 kΩ < Rn < 100 kΩ have EJ < EC and EJ comparable to ℏωp, placing them in the MQT regime where Tesc = ℏωp/7.2kB ≈ 1 K determines switching. This explains why their Is values at 50 mK and 1.5 K are comparable (both below Tesc), whereas thermal activation would produce temperature-dependent switching. The crossover occurs when EC becomes comparable to EJ: binding energy renormalization applies when phase is moderately delocalized (EC/EJ < 1), while MQT escape temperature applies when charging effects dominate (EC > EJ) and the phase tunnels through the barrier.

QA1429.question: Both papers motivate their robust methods by first showing that a natural, simpler baseline estimator fails catastrophically under contamination, then fixing it with a reformulated criterion. Compare the identified failure of each naive baseline and the structural fix each paper applies.
QA1429.answer: RLGP's naive baseline is the standard local GP MLE for the mean, mu_hat = 1^T Sigma^-1 y / 1^T Sigma^-1 1, a weighted average of observed responses; the paper shows even a single rogue point in a heterogeneous local neighborhood can distort this estimate arbitrarily, so RLGP fixes it by subtracting a sparse mean-shift vector gamma from the residuals before forming the weighted average, solved jointly via block coordinate descent (paper1 pp.5,7,9-10). M3VB's naive baseline is direct aggregation of local posteriors via the mean KL divergence (equivalent to averaging m-powered local likelihoods), which the paper shows is non-robust since a single corrupted subset can pull the aggregated posterior arbitrarily far from the truth; replacing the mean with a plain median also fails because the minimizer of median KL divergence does not coincide with the maximizer of median ELBO (since the marginal likelihood terms differ across subsets), so M3VB fixes this with a min-max median formulation that cancels these marginal terms (paper2 pp.31-33). In both cases, the fix involves reformulating the objective (via an auxiliary optimization variable in RLGP, via a min-max dual formulation in M3VB) so that the robust criterion remains aligned with the original well-posed inferential goal (accurate posterior mean estimation).

QA1430.question: Both RLGP and M3VB build robustness around a single scalar controlling the assumed fraction of contaminated data (q in RLGP, alpha_n in M3VB) — how does each method operationalize this parameter within its optimization to neutralize outlier influence, and what is the key structural difference in how the two mechanisms achieve robustness?
QA1430.answer: RLGP encodes robustness through an upper bound q (or q = alpha*n) on the number of nonzero entries of a sparse mean-shift vector gamma, enforced via an l0 constraint; iterative quantile-thresholding (Θ#) solves the resulting nonconvex block-coordinate subproblem by keeping only the q largest-magnitude adjusted residuals as outliers and zeroing the rest, so contaminated observations are individually absorbed and removed from the likelihood contribution. M3VB instead encodes an assumed corruption fraction alpha_n at the level of subsets of data (not individual points): it defines a quantile level tau = (1-2alpha_n)/(2-2alpha_n) and aggregates m local (m-powered) posteriors via a min-max median, so that as long as fewer than half the subsets (up to alpha_n m) are corrupted, the global median of ELBO differences is guaranteed to lie between the tau and 1-tau quantiles of the uncontaminated subsets' loss differences, canceling out corrupted-subset influence entirely rather than down-weighting individual points. Thus RLGP robustifies at the observation level through sparse trimming inside one local regression problem, whereas M3VB robustifies at the subset/block level through quantile-controlled median aggregation across many local optimization problems.

QA1432.question: RLGP and M3VB each modify a standard statistical objective to eliminate a term that would otherwise make direct optimization ill-posed or inconsistent. What is the specific problematic term each paper removes, and what reformulation accomplishes this?
QA1432.answer: RLGP's starting point, the multivariate Gaussian negative log-likelihood (1/2)(y-1mu)^T Sigma^{-1}(y-1mu) + (n/2) log det(Sigma), has no finite lower bound and diverges as Sigma approaches singularity, which would destabilize joint mean/covariance/outlier estimation. RLGP resolves this via a multivariate perspective transformation: introducing S = Sigma^{1/2} and using the jointly convex, lower-bounded surrogate (1/2)(y-1mu)^T S^{-1}(y-1mu) + (1/2) Tr(S), which stays bounded as Sigma -> 0. M3VB's starting point, minimizing the median of per-subset KL divergences KL(Q_theta || m-powered local posterior), is contaminated by the subset-specific marginal likelihood term p-tilde^m(X_j), which varies across j and makes the median-KL minimizer inconsistent with the median-ELBO maximizer. M3VB resolves this via a min-max reformulation, subtracting a second variational distribution G's KL/ELBO from F's, which cancels the p-tilde^m(X_j) terms and restores alignment between the KL minimizer and ELBO maximizer. Both papers therefore use a structural reformulation (perspective transformation for a diverging likelihood; min-max differencing for a subset-dependent normalizing constant) rather than direct regularization, to remove the specific term that made the naive objective ill-posed.

QA1434.question: Both papers report that an approximate theoretical framework breaks down under certain parameter conditions. In each case, does the breakdown of the approximation indicate that the underlying localization phenomenon itself is not real, or something else?
QA1434.answer: In neither case does breakdown of the approximation negate the underlying phenomenon; instead it marks the limits of a scaling ansatz or perturbative expansion that is only valid over a restricted range. In Paper 1, the Thouless-time scaling t_Th = t0 * exp(W/(Omega*L^2)) fits data well at accessible system sizes, but the largest available system sizes in the random XXZ model violate it; this breakdown is interpreted not as proof that MBL is a finite-size illusion, but as a signature that the scaling itself has a limited range of validity and that transport slows further as the true MBL transition is approached. In Paper 2, the superasymptotic Van Vleck expansion for the driven quasiperiodic model achieves accurate agreement with exact dynamics only up to an optimal truncation order, after which resonant hybridizations cause it to diverge; this breakdown does not undercut the localization plateau seen in exact Floquet diagonalization, but instead confirms that the observed localization is a genuinely nonperturbative phenomenon that a divergent asymptotic series can only approximate up to its optimal order.

QA1434.derived_conclusion: In both random-disorder MBL and driven quasiperiodic Floquet localization, breakdown of an approximate scaling law or perturbative expansion is diagnostic of that approximation's restricted range of validity, not evidence against the reality of the localized phase, which in each case is corroborated by independent exact numerics.

QA1435.question: In the random-disorder MBL picture and in the driven quasiperiodic Floquet-localization picture, a supposedly stable localized regime is threatened by rare events that a mean-field-like description misses. What are these rare events in each case, and what do their differing roles imply about whether localization survives?
QA1435.answer: In standard MBL, rare Griffiths regions of anomalously weak disorder seed the avalanche mechanism: a small thermal inclusion can grow and thermalize an arbitrarily long localized chain, ultimately threatening the stability of MBL in the thermodynamic limit. In the driven Aubry-Andre/generalized Aubry-Andre model, the analogous rare events are resonant hybridizations, i.e. anomalously small energy denominators (E_w - E_x + p1omega + p2omega) in the Van Vleck expansion, which proliferate when the underlying spectrum is continuous (weak quasiperiodic potential) and cause the superasymptotic perturbative expansion to break down even though the exact Floquet dynamics still shows a robust localization plateau. So in the MBL case rare events undermine the localized phase itself, whereas in the driven quasiperiodic case rare events only undermine the perturbative description while the true (nonperturbative) localization persists.

In Paper 2, the quasiperiodic potential need not itself be in a localized regime at all; even when the static Aubry-Andre model sits at lambda values where it is delocalized or only weakly disordered, an added staggered periodic drive generates, via the Van Vleck effective Hamiltonian, long-range photon-assisted hopping terms modulated by the quasiperiodic potential, and it is the drive-induced competition between this modulated hopping and the photon-dressed onsite potential -- not Griffiths-region suppression -- that produces the universal localized plateau. Thus the same class of quasiperiodic potential serves as the source of static disorder correlations stabilizing equilibrium MBL in Paper 1, but merely as a spatial modulation ingredient that a drive exploits to build a nonperturbative, resonance-mediated localization in Paper 2.

QA1437.question: The quantum sun model (Paper 1) is used to give clean numerical evidence for a many-body mobility edge in an interacting, static disordered system, while the Floquet quasiperiodic lattice study (Paper 2) shows that periodic driving can erase a single-particle mobility edge (in the generalized Aubry-Andre model) by driving all Floquet eigenstates into a universal localized plateau. In Paper 1, the many-body mobility edge is an equilibrium, static-Hamiltonian feature of the quantum sun model: for interaction strength above criticality (alpha ~ 0.76), only the bulk of the many-body spectrum is ergodic while edge energies stay localized, an effect tied to the density of states of the fixed thermal bath plus localized chain, not to any external drive. In Paper 2, the mobility edge that disappears belongs to the static, single-particle generalized Aubry-Andre model; it is erased specifically by a time-periodic staggered hopping drive that, at a fine-tuned amplitude-to-frequency ratio, produces algebraically decaying long-range hopping in the effective Floquet Hamiltonian that overwhelms the underlying quasiperiodic potential structure and localizes every Floquet state, independent of the undriven spectrum's localization properties. So Paper 2's result is about a driven system suppressing a static single-particle mobility edge via resonant Floquet physics, while Paper 1's mobility edge is an undriven many-body equilibrium phenomenon; neither paper's evidence bears on the other's claim.

QA1438.question: Could the quantum sun model's approach of coupling a localized chain to a finite thermal bath—which exhibits surprisingly small finite-size effects enabling precise determination of mobility edges—be adapted to study Floquet-driven systems where finite-size effects complicate distinguishing genuine universal localization from prethermal plateaus, and what fundamental differences in the sources of ergodicity would limit such a transfer?
QA1438.answer: The quantum sun model achieves exceptional finite-size control by coupling a non-interacting disordered chain to a fixed-size (finite N) GOE random matrix representing a thermal bath, with interaction strength decaying exponentially with distance α; the average gap ratio crosses from Poisson to GOE statistics at a sharply defined critical α≈0.76 with curves for different system sizes L crossing almost at a single point, enabling precise determination of many-body mobility edges as a function of energy density ε. This controlled setup could in principle be extended to Floquet contexts by replacing the static chain Hamiltonian with a periodically driven one, potentially disentangling drive-induced heating from intrinsic localization. However, fundamental differences would limit direct transfer: (1) In the quantum sun model, thermalization arises from a single fixed thermal inclusion (the GOE sun) that can grow to thermalize the chain via avalanche mechanism, whereas in Floquet systems ergodicity emerges from resonant absorption of energy quanta ℏω creating proliferating resonances E_w - E_x ± mω throughout the spectrum when the static part has continuous spectrum; (2) The quantum sun's exponential interaction decay u_j ∝ e^{-αj} creates a well-defined length scale for bath influence, while Floquet systems develop algebraically decaying long-range hopping terms at order 1/ω^{2k} extending to (2k+1)-th neighbors with modulated amplitudes inheriting spatial structure from the disorder; (3) Universal Floquet localization at (a,ω)≈(1,2) persists even when all static eigenstates are delocalized (λ=1) or critical (λ=2), requiring complete cancellation of nearest-neighbor hopping by drive, a mechanism absent in the quantum sun's avalanche-based thermalization. Thus while the quantum sun's finite-size methodology could provide experimental benchmarks, the nonperturbative nature of Floquet localization and its drive-protocol dependence represent qualitatively distinct physics.
QA1438.relation: Paper 1 describes the quantum sun model's exceptional finite-size control enabling precise phase boundary determination; Paper 2 presents universal Floquet localization with complex finite-size behavior and perturbation theory breakdown; assessing transferability requires comparing the mechanisms of ergodicity (thermal bath coupling versus drive-induced resonances) and identifying fundamental incompatibilities.
QA1438.derived_conclusion: While the quantum sun model's controlled finite-bath methodology could provide quantitative benchmarks for Floquet experiments, the fundamentally different ergodicity mechanisms—avalanche thermalization from a localized thermal inclusion versus resonant energy absorption creating spectral hybridization—limit direct theoretical transfer; Floquet systems require nonperturbative understanding of drive-induced long-range hopping that lacks analog in quantum sun's exponentially decaying bath coupling.

QA1439.question: What combination of dynamical signatures—considering imbalance oscillations, gap ratio statistics, and entanglement growth—would enable experimental platforms such as optical lattices to unambiguously distinguish between static quasiperiodic many-body localization (with exponentially sharpening transition and persistent oscillations) and universal Floquet localization at (a,ω)≈(1,2) (with complete dynamical freezing independent of static λ), given that both regimes exhibit localized eigenstates?
QA1439.answer: Distinguishing the two localization mechanisms requires exploiting three key observable differences: (1) Protocol dependence: Static QP-MBL transition occurs at λ_c=2 independent of any drive parameters, with gap ratio derivatives |α_r| flowing exponentially with system size L for both XXZ and kicked Ising models; universal Floquet localization emerges only at the fine-tuned ratio (a,ω)≈(1,2) for staggered/sublattice-asymmetric drive and persists across λ=1 (fully delocalized static), λ=2 (critical static), and λ=3 (localized static), demonstrating drive-induced rather than disorder-induced origin. (2) Dynamical signatures: Static QP-MBL exhibits robust oscillations in imbalance I(t) that persist with increasing L (characteristic of quasi-local integrals of motion), whereas universal Floquet localization shows complete freezing of the local probability density ⟨p_{nT}(j)⟩_g with no temporal evolution beyond initial localization—the wavepacket remains confined to the initial site across all stroboscopic times nT. (3) Spectral statistics sensitivity: For static QP systems, gap ratio ⟨r⟩ transitions from GOE (≈0.5307) to Poisson (≈0.386) with the crossing point drifting logarithmically with L (weaker finite-size effects than random disorder); for universal Floquet localization at (a,ω)=(1,2), all eigenstates collapse to O(1) IPR scaling regardless of static properties and across both sinusoidal and square-wave drive protocols. Experimental protocols should therefore: (i) vary λ at fixed (a,ω)=(1,2) to confirm localization persists into delocalized static regime, (ii) measure long-time stroboscopic dynamics to distinguish persistent oscillations (static MBL) from complete freezing (Floquet), and (iii) scan the (a,ω) plane at fixed λ to map the universal localization plateau's boundaries, which should be independent of the underlying static localization transition.
QA1439.relation: Paper 1 characterizes static quasiperiodic MBL through specific dynamical and spectral signatures including exponentially sharpening transitions and persistent oscillations; Paper 2 establishes universal Floquet localization with complete dynamical freezing independent of static disorder strength; distinguishing these experimentally requires identifying observable differences that isolate drive-induced versus disorder-induced mechanisms.

QA1449.question: Paper 1's robust procurement design introduces a quantity floor to protect the buyer against misspecified cost distributions in a single-seller screening problem. Would an analogous 'floor'-type fix resolve the pure-strategy Nash equilibrium nonexistence documented for Morocco's reference-price procurement rule, and why or why not?

QA1456.question: The SBD paper obtains a tractable HMC sampling target by analytically integrating the image out of the joint blur-image conditional to get a marginal likelihood in the blur alone. The kinetics paper obtains a tractable deterministic description by taking the Θ→0 limit of a Gibbs measure over entire histories rather than integrating out any variable. In the SBD paper, the image c is a genuine nuisance variable with an analytically tractable Gaussian conditional distribution; the paper explicitly integrates p(d,c*|ω,...) over c* to obtain the exact marginal likelihood p(d|ω,...) (Eq. 45), which remains a proper probability density used as an HMC target — no information about the image's distribution is discarded, only its coordinates are removed by exact integration. In the kinetics paper, no variable is integrated out: the full history h=(z0,...,zN) is retained, and the Θ→0 limit is a concentration (Laplace-type) limit of the Gibbs measure P_Θ[h] onto the set M of minimum-action histories, which converts a distribution over the full history space into a (possibly non-unique) deterministic selection rule, discarding the epistemic spread rather than any dimension. Thus marginalization in the SBD paper reduces dimensionality while preserving exact probabilistic content, whereas the Θ→0 limit in the kinetics paper preserves the full history dimensionality while collapsing probabilistic content to a deterministic (or finite-multiplicity) selection.

QA1457.question: Variational Bayes methods in both papers exhibit posterior covariance that is too small or mismatched relative to the true posterior, but for different structural reasons. What are the two distinct mechanisms identified, and how does each paper's proposed fix address its respective mechanism?
QA1457.answer: In Paper 1, the mismatch arises from partitioning data into m subsets: each local posterior built from 1/m of the data has asymptotic covariance m/n·H, far larger than the full posterior's 1/n·H, so naive aggregation understates precision; the fix is raising local likelihoods to the m-th power (or, with local latent variables, using a two-stage aggregate-and-rescale procedure with a 1/m rescaling) to match the full-sample covariance. In Paper 2, the mismatch instead comes from the mean-field factorization assumption itself: forcing q(Θ) to factorize into independent components (e.g., q(β)q(σ2) or q(ω)q(β)q(Σ)...) discards posterior dependence among parameters, so VI/SVI systematically underestimate variances and produce distorted credible intervals even with all the data pooled (no subsetting). Paper 2's remedy is only diagnostic (comparing WAIC/DIC/credible widths to MCMC), not a structural correction like Paper 1's rescaling.
QA1457.relation: Paper 1 alone only explains the subset-aggregation covariance mismatch and its m-power correction; Paper 2 alone only explains mean-field independence causing variance underestimation. Distinguishing the two distinct root causes of undersized VB covariance requires both papers.

QA1459.question: Paper 2's Clustered Hierarchical Linear Regression Model (CHLRM) includes a local latent cluster-assignment variable γ_j for each group, playing a role analogous to the local latent variables S in Paper 1's framework. If one tried to robustly aggregate m disjoint data subsets of a CHLRM-type model by raising each subset's likelihood to the m-th power (as Paper 1 does for models without local latent variables), would this be statistically consistent, and what alternative does Paper 1's theory require in this situation?
QA1459.answer: It would not be consistent. Paper 1 shows that when local latent variables (like S, or analogously CHLRM's γ_j) are present, the m-th power of the marginal likelihood obtained by integrating out the latent variable is generally not proportional to the m-th power of the full marginal likelihood, i.e., fp_m(X|θ) ≠ {p(X|θ)}^m, which makes the population-level minimizer θ*_m differ from the true θ*, biasing the aggregated posterior mean. Since CHLRM's per-group likelihood explicitly depends on the latent cluster indicator γ_j (analogous to S), m-powering it before subset-aggregation would introduce this same bias. Paper 1's remedy is the two-stage 'aggregate-and-rescale' approach: apply min-max median aggregation directly to the unpowered local posteriors and then rescale the resulting distribution's covariance by a factor of 1/m to restore statistical efficiency, rather than raising the local (marginal) likelihood to the m-th power.

QA1461.question: How does the ST-RIS system's use of a single radar waveform type (LFM chirp) for sensing with communication embedded via echo-side phase modulation compare to the Wi-Fi system's exploitation of diverse packet types (data, management, control) with different PHY formats and bandwidths, and what signal processing challenge does the latter introduce that requires a sanitization pipeline not needed in the former?
QA1461.answer: The ST-RIS system transmits a single LFM chirp waveform p(t) = exp(jπκt²) with fixed bandwidth B and pulse repetition interval T_pri. Communication is embedded by the ST-RIS applying time-varying phase modulation β_{m_x,m_y}(t) = φ_{m_x,m_y} + γ(t) to the reflected echo, where spatial phase φ compensates for geometric delays and temporal phase γ(t) carries communication symbols. This produces a consistent waveform structure at the receiver: the beat signal d(t) = μ_s exp[jγ(t-τ)] exp[j(2πf_τ t + θ_τ)], requiring only frequency and phase compensation. In contrast, the Wi-Fi system exploits diverse packet types—data, management (e.g., beacons at ~10 Hz), and control frames (e.g., ACKs, RTS)—which constitute approximately 70% of packets even during video streaming. These packets exhibit heterogeneous PHY formats (802.11n/ac/ax/be), different preamble structures (L-LTF, HT-LTF, VHT-LTF), dynamic bandwidths (20/40/80 MHz), and packet-level amplitude scaling from AGC and transmit power control. This heterogeneity means measured CSI is Ĥ^(p) = α^(p)[S^(p) ⊙ H^(p)] + E^(p), where S^(p) captures format-dependent distortions and α^(p) is unknown gain variation. The sanitization pipeline is therefore required to cluster packets by PHY metadata, normalize amplitudes, align clusters with compatible preambles using coherence-window matching, and filter bursts, converting heterogeneous CSI into unified representations before learning.

QA1462.question: Under a fixed total bandwidth constraint B_T, how does the ST-RIS radar system's explicit sensing-communication bandwidth allocation tradeoff, including the optimal allocation under a sensing constraint, contrast with the Wi-Fi system's claim of zero communication overhead, and what fundamental difference in system architecture enables these divergent resource utilization paradigms?
QA1462.answer: The ST-RIS system exhibits an explicit bandwidth tradeoff B_s + B_c = B_T where sensing bandwidth B_s = κT₀ (chirp bandwidth) and communication bandwidth B_c ≈ (1+h)/T_c compete for total bandwidth B_T. The total Fisher Information I_tot = a(B_T - B_c)² + bB_c² decreases monotonically as B_c increases because a >> b (the chirp extracts more information per unit bandwidth than phase modulation). The optimal communication bandwidth allocation satisfying minimum sensing requirement S_min is β* = [1 - √(1-(1+b/a)(1-S_min))]/(1+b/a). In contrast, the Wi-Fi system introduces zero communication degradation because it exploits existing communication packets without injection—it passively monitors CSI from data, management, and control frames already transmitted for communication purposes across multiple bands (2.4/5 GHz). The architectural difference is that the ST-RIS system uses a single shared waveform for both functions (sensing waveform carries communication via echo modulation), creating direct coupling, whereas the Wi-Fi system separates the functions: communication proceeds normally while sensing passively observes the channel state information from those transmissions.

QA1463.question: Both the ST-RIS echo-side ISAC scheme and the UniFi Wi-Fi sensing framework claim to add a secondary function without perturbing the primary signal or protocol. What is the shared design principle underlying this claim, and what distinct mechanism does each system use to realize it?
QA1463.answer: Both systems adopt the principle of extracting a secondary information stream from a signal or traffic flow that is generated for a primary purpose, rather than modifying that primary signal to embed the secondary function. In the ST-RIS scheme, the radar transmitter radiates an unmodified pure sensing waveform (chirp); the ST-RIS impresses communication phase modulation only on the reflected echo at the receiver side, so the transmitted sensing waveform's range resolution and ambiguity function are preserved. In UniFi, the Wi-Fi network's normal data, management, and control packets already exist for communication purposes; UniFi extracts CSI from these packets passively, without injecting probing/dummy packets, thereby fully preserving communication throughput. The mechanism differs: ST-RIS achieves non-intrusiveness by relocating the modulation to the echo side of a physical channel, while UniFi achieves it by harvesting sensing information opportunistically from existing heterogeneous packet traffic across multiple bands.

QA1464.question: The ST-RIS paper derives a strict Pareto trade-off in which allocating shared bandwidth to communication necessarily degrades sensing accuracy, whereas UniFi reports that fusing more communication resources (frame types, bandwidths, bands) consistently improves sensing accuracy with no analogous penalty. Under what structural difference in resource sharing does each result hold, and are these findings in tension?
QA1464.answer: The two findings are not in tension because they concern different resource-sharing structures. In the ST-RIS system, sensing and communication compete for the same fixed total bandwidth BT = Bs + Bc, so increasing the communication bandwidth fraction β necessarily reduces the chirp bandwidth Bs, and since the chirp waveform extracts more Fisher Information per unit bandwidth than the phase modulation (a > b), total delay-estimation information Itot decreases monotonically as β grows, producing a convex Pareto frontier with no operating point achieving both S~=1 and C~=1. In UniFi, sensing does not compete with communication for a shared spectral resource; it passively harvests CSI that is a byproduct of packets already being transmitted for communication regardless of sensing needs. Consequently, incorporating more frame types within a band or fusing multiple bands only adds independent CSI observations (e.g., fusing 5+2.4 GHz reaches 96.88% accuracy versus 91.43% using only QoS data at 5 GHz) without reducing any communication resource, so there is no zero-sum trade-off analogous to ST-RIS's bandwidth constraint.

Both are necessary because high adaptation accuracy does not guarantee improved task outcomes, and improved task metrics do not reveal whether the system is successfully learning user-specific patterns. A comprehensive evaluation requires both predictive model performance and end-task user experience measures.

QA1484.question: Paper 1 proves CCTS remains PSPACE-complete even when restricted to planar cubic base graphs (Theorem 1, page 10), using padded gadgets (Figure 8) that maintain planarity while ensuring all vertices have degree exactly 3. Paper 2's characterizations rely on treewidth, pathwidth, and treedepth parameters, where Paper 2 cites (page 41) that every n-vertex planar graph has treewidth O(√n) by grid minor theorems. Given that Paper 1's cubic planar base graphs have bounded degree and planarity, why don't these structural restrictions provide polynomial-time algorithms via Paper 2's bounded-width characterizations?
QA1484.answer: The key distinction is that Paper 1 establishes PSPACE-completeness of the decision problem (is a solution sequence of swaps possible?), not the complexity of computing any specific polynomial or function over the graph structure. Paper 1 (page 10, Theorem 1) proves CCTS is PSPACE-complete for cubic planar base graphs with 4-color swap graphs containing P4, meaning determining reachability of configurations requires polynomial space even on these restricted graphs. The padded gadgets in Figure 8 (page 11) maintain planarity and cubic structure while preserving the computational hardness of the configuration-to-configuration reachability problem. Paper 2's results apply to computing homomorphism polynomials: when pattern graphs have bounded treewidth, their homomorphism polynomials admit polynomial-size algebraic circuits (Theorem 6.1, page 21). While Paper 2 notes (page 41, Theorem 8.7) that planar graphs have treewidth O(√n), this doesn't help Paper 1's problem because: (1) CCTS is not about computing a polynomial over the base graph structure, but about state-space reachability through that structure under swap constraints; (2) Paper 1's hardness comes from the exponential number of possible token configurations (n! permutations), not from the base graph complexity; (3) The swap graph (P4 with 4 vertices in Paper 1's hard instances) controls the constraint structure, and Paper 2 shows that even though homomorphism polynomials for small patterns are tractable, the CCTS decision problem requires tracking global configuration states. Paper 1's polynomial-time case (Theorem 8, page 14) for star swap graphs works precisely because equivalence relations under the star constraint structure can be computed efficiently, not because of base graph properties.
QA1484.relation: Paper 1 establishes decision problem complexity for token swapping constrained by graph structure, while Paper 2 establishes polynomial computation complexity for specific graph parameters. Both are needed to understand why bounded graph-theoretic parameters don't automatically yield tractable decision problems.
QA1484.derived_conclusion: Bounded graph-theoretic parameters (treewidth, pathwidth, planarity) of structural graphs (base graphs, swap graphs) do not automatically render decision problems tractable because decision problem complexity depends on configuration space size and constraint interaction, not just on the structural complexity of the constraint topology itself.

QA1485.question: Paper 1's reduction to PSPACE-completeness constructs rigid gadgets (edge, OR, AND) where each gadget operates independently except through connection points, with token movements confined by support constraints. Paper 2 defines rigid symmetric circuits where support size maxSup(C) relates to orbit size via Lemma 2.5, and shows support depth bounds treedepth of computed homomorphism polynomials (Lemma 6.20). How does the notion of 'support' as a constraint mechanism differ between Paper 1's gadget-based reductions and Paper 2's symmetric circuit theory, and what role does rigidity play in establishing complexity bounds in each framework?
QA1485.answer: The term 'support' serves fundamentally different but analogously crucial roles in bounding complexity. In Paper 1 (pages 6-10), the edge, OR, and AND gadgets use support implicitly through connection points: tokens can only interact between gadgets via designated vertices, creating localized state spaces. The gadgets are 'rigid' in that their internal structure uniquely determines behavior—for example, the edge gadget's token of color 4 is confined to vertex x2 or x5 (page 5), creating a support constraint that forces specific traversal patterns. This structural rigidity enables the PSPACE-hardness proof by ensuring NCL edge orientations faithfully correspond to gadget configurations. In Paper 2 (page 8), rigidity means something precise: a symmetric circuit C is rigid if the only automorphism fixing all input gates is the identity (Lemma 2.4), enabling well-defined support sets sup(g) for each gate g. The support sup(g) ⊆ [n] ⊎ [n] is the minimal set whose pointwise stabilizer Stab•(S) is a subgroup of Stab(g). Lemma 2.5 (page 9) establishes that polynomial orbit size is equivalent to constant maximum support size. Crucially, Lemma 6.20 (page 31) proves that support depth—how often supports change along circuit paths—bounds the treedepth of pattern graphs whose homomorphism polynomials are computed. In both papers, rigidity eliminates structural redundancy to enable precise complexity analysis: Paper 1 uses it to maintain bijections between NCL configurations and token arrangements; Paper 2 uses it to bound orbit sizes via support sizes, which then bound pattern graph parameters and thus complexity classes.

QA1486.question: Discretization approximation (DA) and unadjusted Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (uHMC) are both proposed as alternatives or complements to standard MCMC for Bayesian computation. QA1491.question: Both the GNN pooling study and the gene-regulatory knock-in study compute a gene's 'importance' from a locally-defined operation, yet both papers note that this local score may not capture the gene's full network-level effect. In contrast, the knock-in paper shows that the biologically meaningful effect of perturbing a single gene is not fully captured at distance 1 alone, since the influence of a knock-in propagates through the network and must be traced to distance 2, 3, and beyond, with genes like Med23 or Ppara showing their most substantial restorative effects (up to 10% of lost information) only once these longer-range pairs are included, even as the effect per pair diminishes with distance. QA1494.question: How does the choice to binarize gene expression data enable complementary but distinct forms of network analysis in graph neural network architectures versus binary state regulatory models, and what computational versus biological information trade-offs does this methodological choice impose?
QA1494.answer: Binarization serves different but complementary purposes in the two frameworks: In GNNs, the TCGA data are binarized to handle sparsity in single-cell RNA-seq where many genes in many cells have no detected transcripts, incorporating the experimental detection threshold naturally (0=off/undetected, 1=on/detected) and making results agnostic to upstream processing choices that never change zero/nonzero status. This enables training on 14,133 genes across 7,008 tumor and 701 normal samples. In the binary regulation model, binarization enables analytic tractability: the four probabilities (p00, p01, p10, p11) for each TF-TG pair allow closed-form parameter inference (α, β, γ) via simple equations and direct mutual information calculation (I = Σpij log[pij/(qirj)]), making analysis of 6,253 regulatory pairs computationally efficient without iterative optimization. The trade-off is loss of granular expression information: the GNN sacrifices capturing quantitative expression differences within the "on" state, potentially limiting modeling capacity, while the binary model's simplicity prevents it from representing gradual regulatory responses, causing information to vanish at maximum expression (I→0 as pon→1 for direct pairs). However, binarization enables both approaches to scale to genome-wide networks with thousands of genes, which would be computationally prohibitive with continuous models requiring extensive fitting or iterative training on sparse high-dimensional data.
QA1494.relation: Paper 1 applies binarization to handle experimental data sparsity in GNNs, while Paper 2 uses binarization to achieve analytic tractability in regulatory modeling. Understanding the full implications requires both papers to establish how this shared methodological choice enables different computational advantages while imposing comparable limitations on biological information capture.
QA1494.derived_conclusion: Binarizing gene expression data represents a strategic methodological convergence that prioritizes computational scalability and analytical tractability over quantitative precision: it enables both deep learning on sparse experimental data and closed-form theoretical analysis of network perturbations, but at the cost of collapsing expression heterogeneity within "on" states, revealing a fundamental trade-off between model complexity and the ability to analyze genome-scale biological networks with thousands of regulatory interactions.

The GNN's pre-computed approach sacrifices adaptability for tractability when handling 14,133-node networks, while the binary model's direct inference enables rapid parameter calculation across 6,253 regulatory pairs without iterative optimization. For large gene networks, the GNN's fixed clustering prevents learning optimal gene groupings during training, whereas the binary model's analytic solution allows efficient exploration of single-gene perturbations across the entire network by propagating effects through recursive steady-state calculations.

QA1497.question: Both papers use linear structural equation modeling (LSEM) to decompose treatment effects into direct and indirect (mediated) components, but they differ in how rigorously they establish identification of the indirect/mediated pathway. How do the identification approaches compare, and what assumption does the hypertension mediation paper make explicit that the life-course SEM paper leaves unformalized?
QA1497.answer: The hypertension trial paper explicitly formalizes identification of the natural indirect effect through a set of causal assumptions (SUTVA, positivity, consistency, treatment ignorability, and sequential ignorability under single-world intervention graphs), and proves that its conditional average indirect/direct effects are identified from observed data under these assumptions plus the LSEM parametric form. This sequential ignorability assumption states that, conditional on treatment and covariates, the potential outcome under a given mediator value is independent of the mediator's potential value under the assigned treatment, i.e. no unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding. In contrast, the life-course SEM paper estimates an analogous mediated pathway (education mediating childhood SES's effect on adult SES) purely via path coefficients estimated by maximum likelihood in a cross-lagged SEM, without stating or invoking any ignorability-type assumption for the mediator-outcome relationship; identification there rests only on model fit and temporal ordering of observed variables. Thus the hypertension paper grounds its mediated effect in explicit counterfactual identification conditions, while the life-course paper treats the analogous decomposition as a standard regression-based path estimate without addressing mediator-outcome confounding.

QA1535.question: SLAM-LLM's audio captioning evaluation and VeriTAS's fact-checking evaluation both propose metrics beyond simple accuracy. How do the error-cost assumptions embedded in SLAM-LLM's FENSE/SPIDEr-style captioning metrics differ from those embedded in VeriTAS's MSE-based scoring, and what does this reveal about matching a metric to a task's error severity structure?
QA1535.answer: SLAM-LLM evaluates audio captioning with metrics like METEOR, CIDEr, SPICE, SPIDEr, and FENSE, which combine n-gram/semantic overlap with fluency-error detection to reward captions that are both semantically aligned and grammatically sound, treating quality as a graded, largely symmetric similarity judgment between generated and reference text (merged p.9). VeriTAS instead scores each claim property on a continuous −1 to +1 scale and uses Mean Squared Error as its primary metric specifically because squaring the difference strongly penalizes 'flipped' predictions (e.g., calling a Compromised claim Intact) while treating near-misses involving uncertainty (NEI) leniently; an MSE of 0.04 is called 'very high agreement' while an MSE near 1.0 is equivalent to constant NEI prediction (merged p.6-7, p.21-22). This contrast shows that captioning quality is treated as a continuous similarity/fluency problem where no single error is catastrophic, whereas fact-checking verdict prediction treats sign-reversal errors as categorically severe (a true claim mislabeled false, or vice versa), so the metric must disproportionately punish such flips rather than just measure average deviation.
QA1535.relation: Answering requires citing SLAM-LLM's specific AAC metric suite and rationale and VeriTAS's specific MSE rationale and interpretation table; neither paper alone explains why a task's error-cost structure should dictate metric choice.
QA1535.derived_conclusion: Metric design in LLM-based generation/verification systems should reflect the task's underlying error-cost asymmetry: symmetric similarity metrics suit open-ended generation like captioning, while squared-error metrics that heavily penalize sign flips suit binary-stakes verification like fact-checking.

QA1539.question: Do the axioms characterizing IATA's weighted flights rule (additivity, independence of other airlines, and ratio preservation) guarantee immunity to strategic manipulation analogous to click-fraud proofness in music streaming platforms?
QA1539.answer: No, the axioms characterizing IATA's weighted flights rule do not guarantee immunity to strategic manipulation analogous to click-fraud proofness. Click-fraud proofness in music streaming requires that an artist cannot profit from generating fake streams beyond the subscription fee, which is satisfied by user-centric but not pro-rata. Similarly, IATA's weighted proportional rule is vulnerable when airlines can artificially inflate their flight counts or weights. The axioms ensure consistent allocation principles (such as separability across passengers and preservation of relative shares) but are silent on robustness against endogenous manipulation of the inputs (flights or streams) themselves. QA1540.question: Papers 1 and 2 both rely on incentive compatibility (IC) as a binding constraint when designing procurement mechanisms under unknown seller cost, yet reach their worst-case-optimal schedules through different objectives (welfare-guarantee-then-conjectured-model vs. competitive ratio). Does the absence of IC in Paper 3's rule create a conflict with the design principles common to Papers 1 and 2, and how is that conflict manifested in the equilibrium analysis?
QA1540.answer: Yes. Papers 1 and 2 treat IC as a structural constraint that any candidate mechanism must satisfy before its worst-case performance is even evaluated: Paper 1's short list MSL is defined only over mechanisms M=(q,u) that are IC and IR, and Paper 2's transfer schedules are indirect mechanisms derived via the taxation principle so that the seller's optimal quantity choice under any realized cost is well defined and truth-telling-equivalent. Paper 3's Moroccan rule imposes no such constraint: the reference price P is a function of all bids' average, so a bidder's payoff depends discontinuously and non-monotonically on their own report relative to others' reports, with no schedule ensuring that reporting 'truthfully' (whatever that would mean here, since there is no private cost type being elicited via a menu) is a best response. This absence of an IC-compatible allocation rule is exactly what produces the conflict: because every non-winning bidder can always find a strictly improving deviation (undercutting to become closest to P from below), no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium exists, whereas the IC-restricted mechanisms of Papers 1 and 2 are constructed precisely so that deterministic best responses (truthful reporting, or optimal quantity choice given the cost-contingent transfer) exist and are stable.

QA1541.question: Across the three papers, procurement design under unknown seller cost is handled by three distinct criteria — a worst-case welfare guarantee combined with conjectured-model selection, a competitive-ratio (constant-share) guarantee, and a fixed non-incentive reference-price rule taken directly from Moroccan regulation. QA1542.question: Each paper achieves robustness to outliers or heterogeneous data through a distinct mechanism embedded directly in its estimation objective rather than through post-hoc filtering. How do the three mechanisms differ in what they parameterize as 'atypical,' and what single unifying principle do they share?
QA1542.answer: Paper 1's ALDRM handles heterogeneity by letting the skewness parameter τ (and thus the mode-location parameter) vary with covariates and random effects, so robustness comes from directly modeling asymmetry/heavy tails rather than removing points; the AL quantile loss ρτ makes estimation median/quantile-robust by construction (merged pages 4, 7). Paper 2's RLGP instead parameterizes outlyingness explicitly as a per-observation mean-shift vector γ, estimated jointly with GP hyperparameters under an ℓ0 sparsity constraint that bounds how many points can be flagged as anomalous within a local neighborhood (merged pages 33-34, 36). Paper 3's M3VB instead relocates robustness to the aggregation stage: rather than modeling per-observation asymmetry or outlyingness, it replaces the mean KL divergence used to combine subset posteriors with a min-max median formulation across the m local subsets, so that a minority of corrupted subsets cannot dominate the aggregated posterior (merged pages 57-59). The unifying principle across all three is that robustness is achieved by embedding an explicit, estimable 'nuisance' quantity for deviation (asymmetry/skewness parameter, sparse mean-shift vector, or a median-based aggregator across units) directly into the optimization criterion, rather than assuming a single homogeneous Gaussian error structure.

QA1570.question: How do preprocessing strategies for spatial network modeling compare to optimization-based robustification in terms of computational bottlenecks, and what architectural principles determine when upfront data structuring versus iterative parameter refinement is more efficient?
QA1570.answer: S3N demonstrates that efficient preprocessing—building stream network adjacency in O(r) time by directly extracting node coordinates rather than computing pairwise distances—removes the O(r²) bottleneck present in SSNbler, reducing Network 5 preprocessing from 50-200× slower than S3N to 1 minute for 169,092 reaches. However, pairwise distance computation (1.78 minutes of 2.02 total) remains the dominant cost, parallelizable but requiring all-pairs evaluation. In contrast, RLGP's optimization-based robustification avoids explicit construction of m-powered local posteriors through a joint min-max formulation, achieving competitive O(n) estimation per iteration through gradient-based block coordinate descent with iterative quantile thresholding at each γ-update. The M³VB framework further demonstrates that reformulating aggregation as joint optimization over KL divergences—rather than computing and aggregating m explicit posterior distributions—eliminates the need for expensive metrics over probability spaces. The architectural principle is that when data relationships (e.g., network topology) are fixed and reusable across predictions, upfront preprocessing amortizes cost, but when relationships are test-point-dependent or involve probability distributions, iterative optimization that avoids materializing intermediate structures is more efficient.

QA1572.question: If one wanted to replace the residual-loss component used inside the Robust Local Gaussian Process's block-coordinate optimization with an alternative robustness/asymmetry mechanism, would the GMQ-smoothed quantile loss or the asymmetric Laplace distributional model be the more natural fit, given how each is structured for optimization?
QA1572.answer: The GMQ-smoothed loss is the more compatible substitute. RLGP's objective l(µ,γ,S) is built so that, with any block of parameters fixed, the remaining sub-problems are smooth and convex (the γ-subproblem uses a convex quadratic surrogate g(γ,γ⁻) that majorizes l, and the (µ,S) block is solved via closed-form or gradient/quasi-Newton updates), which is exactly what makes its block-coordinate-descent algorithm converge with monotone objective decrease. The GMQ loss ρτ,c(u) is likewise constructed to be globally convex and infinitely smooth for any positive shape parameter c, yielding a smooth convex empirical risk with algebraic (not transcendental) derivatives—properties that plug naturally into a gradient-based block update in place of RLGP's Gaussian residual term. In contrast, the ALDRM's asymmetry mechanism is not a deterministic convex loss at all: it specifies Y|r ~ AL(µ,σ,τ) and is estimated via a hierarchical Bayesian Gaussian-mixture representation with MCMC (JAGS) sampling, a full likelihood/latent-variable scheme rather than a differentiable convex penalty. Swapping this in for RLGP's residual term would replace RLGP's deterministic convex block-coordinate/quantile-thresholding algorithm with a stochastic sampling procedure, breaking the optimization structure (convex surrogate majorization, monotone decrease guarantee) that RLGP's convergence theorem relies on. Hence GMQ's smooth convex loss is structurally compatible with RLGP's optimization framework, while ALDRM's Bayesian AL-mixture asymmetry model is not.

QA1573.question: Across the GMQ-smoothed quantile regression, the asymmetric Laplace distributional regression model, and the Robust Local Gaussian Process, each method introduces a parameter that governs adaptation to non-Gaussian/heterogeneous behavior in the data (smoothing, asymmetry, or outlyingness). QA1573.answer: The three methods place their key adaptation parameter at three different, increasingly fine granularities. In GMQ quantile regression, the shape parameter c is a single scalar shared by every observation in the sample; its asymptotically optimal value c* is derived from population-level moments of the density and its derivative, so the same smoothing/bias-variance tradeoff applies uniformly across all subjects and data points. In the asymmetric Laplace distributional regression model (ALDRM), the skewness parameter τij is not fixed but is modeled via a logit link with fixed effects and a subject-specific random effect ai, so asymmetry is allowed to vary by individual and over time, i.e., adaptation occurs at the individual (subject) level. In the Robust Local Gaussian Process, the outlyingness vector γ and its sparsity bound q are defined per test location, over the local neighborhood Dn(x*) of nearest neighbors; adaptation is neighborhood-specific and even re-estimated for every new test point. This produces a granularity hierarchy: a single global constant (GMQ), a subject-varying random-effect parameter (ALDRM), and a per-neighborhood, per-test-point sparse adjustment (RLGP), reflecting progressively more localized mechanisms for absorbing heterogeneity that cannot be captured by a single fixed loss or distributional form.

QA1574.question: In each of the three papers, a naive mean-based estimator can be arbitrarily distorted by a single anomalous unit (a data point, a neighbor, or a data subset). Identify the vulnerable mean estimator in each paper and the sparsity- or order-based correction mechanism each proposes, and explain what differs about the quantity each mechanism ultimately protects.
QA1574.answer: All three papers diagnose the same failure mode—an unweighted mean-type estimator can be dragged arbitrarily far by one bad unit—but apply the fix to different targets. In Paper 1, the residual mean/std used to build the Prediction Residual Confidence Interval is a weighted average of squared/absolute residuals in a regression window; a single gross outlier can 'mask' a genuine drift by skewing this residual mean, so the dual-channel process protects the drift-detection statistic by first filtering point outliers with a warning/outlier threshold before residuals are passed to the EWMAD-DT drift channel. In Paper 2, the maximum likelihood estimate of the local mean µ is a weighted average of neighborhood responses y; a single rogue neighbor (e.g., from an adjacent region) can distort µ, so RLGP introduces a sparse outlyingness vector γ with an ℓ0 constraint (∥γ∥0 ≤ q) that absorbs each anomalous response's contribution, protecting the local GP mean function used for prediction at a test location. In Paper 3, the naive aggregation of local (variational) posteriors is itself a form of averaging across subsets; even one corrupted subset can pull the aggregated posterior arbitrarily far from the truth, so M3VB replaces the mean KL divergence across subsets with a min-max median formulation, protecting the mean of the aggregated global-parameter posterior. Thus the protected quantity moves from a scalar residual statistic (Paper 1), to a local regression-function value (Paper 2), to a distributed posterior mean over a global parameter (Paper 3), but in each case a sparse/order-statistic-based device (thresholded warning/outlier flag, ℓ0-sparse γ, and median-of-subsets) is substituted for a plain arithmetic mean to neutralize the single-unit vulnerability.

QA1575.question: Each of the three frameworks specifies a limit on how much local contamination its robustness mechanism can tolerate before breaking down. How do the outlier-level threshold in the dual-channel stream detector, the trimming bound on the RLGP outlyingness vector, and the contamination-fraction condition in the min-max median variational Bayes estimator differ in what kind of quantity they bound, and what common numerical ceiling do the latter two share?

Paper 3's M3VB requires the corrupted-subset fraction to satisfy α_n∈[0,1/2−δ) for some fixed δ, i.e. a strict-margin bound below 50% of subsets. QA1580.question: LARGE, RLGP, and M3VB all rely on structurally similar alternating/block-coordinate optimization schemes to handle a biconvex or nonconvex objective introduced by their adaptivity or robustness mechanism. Do these papers make consistent claims about convergence guarantees for these algorithms, or is there a conflict in the scope of what is actually proven?
QA1580.answer: There is no conflict in claims, but there is a real disparity in the scope of convergence guarantees despite similar algorithmic structure. RLGP proves a formal convergence guarantee: Theorem 3 shows that its block-coordinate-descent iterates (alternating over µ, the sparse outlier vector γ via quantile thresholding, and kernel hyperparameters) produce a monotonically decreasing objective value, ensuring convergence (merged page 31). LARGE, whose BCD loop alternates a nodewise Autotune Lasso regression with adaptive penalty updates, only observes empirical convergence within about 20 iterations and explicitly identifies 'a rigorous convergence analysis of the block coordinate descent algorithm with a biconvex objective in the inner loop' as an open question left for future work (merged page 16), and in practice required relaxing the convergence threshold for harder settings (merged page 13). M3VB goes further in stating a limitation: although it proves strong non-asymptotic statistical (KL divergence) guarantees for the resulting posterior, its concluding remarks explicitly note that the coordinate-ascent-based min-max median algorithm 'lacks theoretical guarantees for convergence to near-optimal solutions' because the min-max median objective is non-convex and non-smooth (merged page 77). So among the three, only RLGP has a proven algorithmic convergence guarantee; LARGE and M3VB both rely on empirical or statistical justification while leaving formal optimization convergence as unresolved.
QA1580.relation: Resolving whether the three structurally analogous algorithms are on equal theoretical footing requires directly comparing LARGE's stated open problem, RLGP's proven monotonic-decrease theorem, and M3VB's explicit disclaimer about its algorithm's convergence guarantees.
QA1580.derived_conclusion: Despite sharing an alternating/block-coordinate optimization design for handling biconvex or nonconvex adaptivity/robustness objectives, only RLGP among the three papers has a formally proven algorithmic convergence guarantee; LARGE and M3VB explicitly flag algorithmic convergence as unresolved even though M3VB proves distributional statistical guarantees for its resulting posterior.

QA1581.question: Each paper studies a map recording monodromy or holonomy of a geometric structure (curve monodromy, oper holonomy, circle monodromy). When are these maps injective, and what auxiliary datum must be fixed to restore injectivity where it fails?
QA1581.answer: In Paper 1, the monodromy map mu:D_3(C)->G is far from injective: for a fixed positive hyperbolic element g, the fiber mu^{-1}(g) has at least four components of convex curves (one per positive triangle of the g-invariant triangulation of S^2), plus additional non-convex components; however, fixing the homotopy class (i.e. passing to the quotient Y_3(C) of curves modulo isomonodromic deformation) makes the map to a single component canonical, and within a fixed component any convex curve is isomonodromically deformable to the model curve t->g^t.v (Proposition 2.12(c)). In Paper 3, the analogous circle monodromy map D_q (equivalently its lift to the universal cover, D'_q) is shown to be a submersion (Proposition 2.2) onto an open subset G-tilde^+ of the universal cover of G, so it again has non-trivial fibers in general, and the space Y_n(C) is precisely introduced as the quotient recording the extra homotopy-class datum needed to distinguish curves with the same monodromy. In Paper 2, the oper holonomy map Hol: Op_X(G) -> Hom(pi_1(X),G)/G is never globally injective as X varies (a fact attributed to Goldman), but Theorem 3.8 proves it is injective once the Riemann surface structure X is fixed, using the osculating map to show any two opers sharing a holonomy over the same compact X must be gauge-equivalent. In all three cases, the monodromy/holonomy map fails to be injective globally but becomes injective, or at least has classifiable finite/structured fibers, once one fixes an auxiliary rigidifying datum: a homotopy class of curve (Papers 1 and 3, encoded by Y_n(C)) or a fixed underlying Riemann surface X (Paper 2).

QA1581.derived_conclusion: Across all three constructions, monodromy/holonomy maps for nondegenerate curves or opers are generically non-injective, and injectivity (or classifiable fibers) is restored only after fixing an auxiliary datum: a homotopy class of curve (via the space Y_n(C) in Papers 1 and 3) or the underlying Riemann surface structure (Paper 2).

QA1587.question: NBQC, the UAV-CPN, and DAVOS all incorporate an explicit runtime mechanism for detecting when a subsystem is becoming a bottleneck so that resources can be reallocated. Compare how each system operationally defines 'bottleneck' and what signal it monitors to trigger reallocation.
QA1587.answer: NBQC's Bottleneck Identification subroutine evaluates, for each remote operation, how long it had to wait for Bell-pair generation due to insufficient QQ- or QF-links (w^QQ and w^QF values); a nonzero wait signals a bottleneck, and the Update NBQC Configuration subroutine then adds links to the pair of components offering the largest execution-time improvement per added node. The UAV-CPN detects a bottleneck by comparing accumulated transmission latency (t1+t2) and CN computing latency against the residual time budget: if t1+t2 exceeds Tmax the system is comm-limited, and if computing latency exceeds the residual budget it is comp-limited; this classification then guides which of altitude or transmit power should be adjusted. DAVOS's real-time scheduling tracking component instead monitors a continuous confidence signal (based on data staleness and fusion misalignment) rather than a binary wait/latency measure; when smoothed confidence indicators fall below thresholds, the system issues regulation requests that trigger local deadline reduction or escalate to the global scheduler for core reallocation. All three thus tie a monitored runtime signal to a corrective resource action, but the signal is a discrete link-wait time in NBQC, a latency-budget comparison in the UAV-CPN, and a continuous confidence metric in DAVOS.

QA1588.question: NBQC, the UAV-CPN, and DAVOS each face a situation where a slow communication or data-transfer step threatens to dominate end-to-end latency. The UAV-CPN falls under spatial/parameter reconfiguration: since the bottleneck between GU-to-UAV offloading, UAV-to-CN forwarding, and CN computation shifts with UAV altitude and transmit power (producing comm-limited or comp-limited regimes), the system resolves the bottleneck not by adding hardware but by jointly re-tuning altitude and transmit power to reshape which CNs are reachable within the latency budget. DAVOS's SIM falls under structural path elimination: because the ROS2/DDS publish-subscribe chain's (de)serialization and copying is itself the source of latency and jitter, SIM removes that path entirely by placing sensor data directly into algorithm-native shared memory, rather than concealing or reallocating around the delay. Each system's category is dictated by whether its bottleneck resource (entanglement generation, wireless/computing coverage, or serialization overhead) can be pre-generated ahead of need, geometrically reshaped, or bypassed altogether.

QA1592.question: Each paper identifies a distinct mechanism that protects or removes a geometric/topological quantity under some deformation. How do the protection criteria used in the three papers differ in what plays the role of the 'deformation' and what determines whether the quantity survives it?
QA1592.answer: All three works pose an invariance question but answer it with different kinds of deformation and different protection criteria. In the light-induced-magnetization theory, the deformation is a change of crystalline symmetry of the material: the response to linearly polarized light, sigma^LPL_zab, is forced to vanish whenever the system simultaneously has a mirror plane perpendicular to it and an n-fold rotation axis (n not equal 2); breaking either symmetry is what 'deforms' the system enough to allow a nonzero response, while circularly polarized light response is never constrained by these symmetries. In the shandite study, the deformation is a change of magnetic texture: under noncoplanar spin configurations the Weyl topology (Type-I character, opposite Chern numbers) remains completely unperturbed regardless of the spin-chiral interaction strength, whereas under noncollinear (spin-spiral) textures the same Weyl nodes are driven through genuine topological phase transitions, first to Type-II and eventually to a gapped state, as the spiral wavelength shortens. In the spectroscopy framework, the deformation is a measurement-induced map from the true band projector to an effective projector built from a finite set of experimental probe states; topological invariants (Chern numbers, Z2 monopole charges) survive this deformation exactly because the map constitutes a smooth vector-bundle isomorphism whenever the no-rank-drop condition holds, even though the local geometric density (Berry curvature, quantum metric) is generally altered. Thus the three protection criteria are: a crystalline symmetry selection rule (Paper 1), an intrinsic-topology robustness against specific classes of magnetic texture but not others (Paper 2), and a rank-preservation condition guaranteeing bundle isomorphism under probe-space projection (Paper 3); only the last is a strict mathematical topological guarantee, while the first is symmetry-dependent and the second depends on which texture class is applied.

QA1594.question: The three papers each build a form of robustness against outliers or heavy-tailed/asymmetric error into a regression procedure, but the mechanism by which robustness is achieved differs structurally. How would you classify the robustness mechanism used in each paper?
QA1594.answer: The three papers achieve robustness through three structurally distinct mechanisms. Paper 1 uses explicit exclusion: a dual-channel decision process computes a Prediction Residual Confidence Interval and flags a point as a warning outlier once the residual exceeds mean+2 standard deviations, and as a confirmed outlier once it exceeds mean+2.6 standard deviations, physically filtering these points out of the regression window before drift detection proceeds. Paper 2 achieves robustness through loss-shape engineering: its GMQ loss's second derivative decays algebraically as O(|x|^-3) rather than exponentially (as in Gaussian-kernel convolution smoothing), so points with large residuals continue to contribute meaningfully, but boundedly, to the curvature estimate used by the Barzilai-Borwein optimizer, rather than being discarded. Paper 3 achieves robustness through distributional accommodation: it models the response as following an asymmetric Laplace distribution whose location parameter is the mode, inheriting the median-based robustness of quantile regression, so outliers and skewness are absorbed into the fitted scale and skewness parameters rather than removed or reweighted. Thus the taxonomy is: exclusion-based filtering (Paper 1), bounded-influence loss curvature (Paper 2), and distributional/parametric absorption (Paper 3).

In KANELÉ, pruning and quantization move essentially all computation into precomputed LUTs, so the online step is reduced to LUT lookups and pipelined additions with no per-inference model-based computation or coordination step at all. QA1599.question: Across the residual-based, GAN-based, and wavelet-HOS-based approaches, each defines a continuous scalar to quantify deviation from a nominal/feasible state, but they set decision boundaries on that scalar in fundamentally different ways. How do the three methods' threshold mechanisms differ in origin (physics-derived optimum vs. empirical validation tuning vs. analytic statistical calibration)?
QA1599.answer: RPF quantifies infeasibility with the residual norm ρ(v;u), and rather than setting a fixed threshold on it, drives ρ toward zero by adjusting a slack variable u_s in the optimization min_{u_s}[min_v ρ(v;u)], so the 'decision boundary' is the physics-derived optimum ρ=0 achieved through control adjustment. GAN-LSTM instead computes an anomaly score S(x) combining residual and discriminator feature losses and picks a scalar threshold τ empirically by sweeping candidate values on a held-out validation set to maximize F1-score, then fixes and applies that same τ to test data. WPT+HOS takes a third route: it models the nominal noise signature f as Gaussian, computes the squared Mahalanobis distance D²(f), and derives an analytic decision threshold η = F⁻¹_{χ²_d}(1−α) from the chi-square null distribution for a chosen false-alarm probability α, giving a statistically calibrated (not empirically tuned) boundary. Thus the three papers represent distinct philosophies for the same underlying task of turning a continuous deviation score into a decision: optimize-to-zero via physical control, tune-on-data, and calibrate-from-a-parametric-null-model.
